883.title: The stone Buddhas
883.hook: at Gal Vihara in Polonnaruwa, great Buddhas carved from one rock, standing, seated, lying
883.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Gal Vihara remove their shoes, offer flowers and sit or stand quietly before the figures; in Buddhist temples, seated and reclining images serve as a focus for meditation and devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Buddhaghosa, and a whole book built on one verse. Your line: the commentator.

A long face of granite, in the old royal city of Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka. Out of it, sculptors cut the Buddha: seated in meditation, standing with arms folded, and lying on his side. Nothing was carried in and set in place. The figures were uncovered, the stone around them cut away, so that each one is still part of the hill. The place is called Gal Vihara, the rock monastery.
screen: `ONE FACE OF GRANITE.` → `SEATED, STANDING, LYING.` → `GAL VIHARA.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The later chronicle credits King Parakramabahu with rebuilding Polonnaruwa as a royal city of parks, reservoirs and monasteries, and with the rock monastery itself. Second, the seated Buddha. He sits in meditation, hands resting in his lap, with a calm the stone holds without effort. Behind him the rock is carved with small details, as if he sits in a shrine of his own. Third, the standing figure, arms folded across his chest. Who is he? People disagree. Some say the Buddha himself, in the days after his awakening. Others say Ananda, his companion and attendant, standing in grief beside his dying teacher. The stone doesn't say, and the debate is still open. Fourth, the lying Buddha. In the account of the Buddha's last days, the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, he lies down on his right side, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clear, between two sal trees. The great reclining figure lies just that way, his head on a pillow. Some see a sleeping Buddha. Others see the final passing. The chronicle doesn't say why the sculptors chose to work in a single rock. What the stone shows is simple: nothing is stacked or joined. The figures share one body with the hill. And a stone Buddha does not fidget, does not check the time, does not shift its weight. Part of what people come for is to sit near that stillness.
screen: `A KING'S ROCK MONASTERY.` · `SEATED, IN MEDITATION.` · `STANDING: THE BUDDHA, OR ANANDA?` · `LYING ON HIS RIGHT SIDE.` · then, large: `CARVED FROM ONE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Find a steady seat, hands resting in your lap, back upright the way stone is upright without trying, and for a while try not to adjust. When an itch or the urge to shift comes, see whether it can pass the way weather passes over rock; if you need to move, move gently, and settle again.
Gal Vihara. The rock monastery at Polonnaruwa where the Buddha was cut seated, standing and lying from a single face of granite. Today's word.
Your line: carved from one rock. Seated, standing and lying, all one hill. See you tomorrow.

884.title: The tooth relic
884.hook: the Buddha's tooth relic, guarded in Kandy
884.howItsDone: At the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, monks hold rituals for the relic and pilgrims offer flowers and incense, and the Esala Perahera procession carries a relic casket through the city's streets.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gal Vihara, Buddhas cut from a single face of granite. Your line: carved from one rock.

After the Buddha's cremation, the Mahaparinibbana Sutta says, his relics nearly started a war. Kings and clans arrived from all sides, each demanding a share. Then a brahmin named Dona spoke up. The Buddha taught patience, he reminded them; it would not be right to come to blows over the remains of such a teacher. So the relics were divided, and each share went home to be honored in a stupa. Sri Lankan tradition says one tooth took a longer road, and it ends in a temple in Kandy.
screen: `THE RELICS NEARLY START A WAR.` → `DONA: HE TAUGHT PATIENCE.` → `ONE TOOTH, A LONGER ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the journey. The chronicle of the tooth, the Dathavamsa, tells how the tooth was kept in India and then, in a time of danger, sent across the sea. A princess named Hemamala and a prince named Dantha, the story says, carried it to Sri Lanka hidden in her hair. Second, the guarding. On the island, the tooth became bound up with kingship. The chronicles describe kings building shrines for it near their palaces and taking it with them when the capital moved. Whoever kept the tooth safe, tradition held, had a claim to rule. Third, Kandy. The relic is kept today in the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, the Sri Dalada Maligawa. Monks perform rituals for it, and pilgrims bring flowers. The tooth rests inside nested caskets and is not usually shown. People honor what they cannot see. Fourth, the procession. In the festival called the Esala Perahera, a casket representing the relic is carried through the streets of Kandy on an elephant, with drummers and dancers all around. What does honoring a relic mean? Buddhists explain it in different ways: a reminder of the Buddha, a focus for devotion, a link to a real person who walked and taught. And the sutta's own scene is worth keeping: the Buddha's remains almost started a fight, and a reminder of his teaching on patience stopped it.

Remember who gave it, or what it holds, and with each breath simply honor it, the way pilgrims in Kandy bring flowers to a casket they never see opened.

885.title: Bagan
885.hook: thousands of temples on the plain of Bagan in Myanmar
885.howItsDone: Buddhists in Myanmar visit the temples of Bagan to offer flowers, candles and food, walk barefoot through the shrines, and dedicate the merit of their giving to their families and to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: datha, the tooth relic, guarded in Kandy. Your line: kept safe.

Dawn, on a wide dry plain beside the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar. As the mist thins, shapes rise out of it: temples and stupas of red brick and white plaster, some enormous, some no bigger than a garden shed, scattered as far as the eye can reach. The plain is quiet, except for a bell somewhere, a broom on a step, a few early visitors taking off their sandals at a doorway. The donors who paid for these buildings called them gifts, and some carved their wishes in stone.
screen: `DAWN BESIDE THE IRRAWADDY.` → `TEMPLES AS FAR AS THE EYE CAN SEE.` → `BAGAN.`

segments.voice: First, the king and the monk. The Burmese chronicles tell how King Anawrahta of Bagan met a monk named Shin Arahan, who taught him the Theravada teaching. They say the king wanted the scriptures and monks of Thaton, a kingdom to the south, and when its king refused him, he went to war and brought them back. Historians question parts of that story, but it is how the tradition remembers Bagan's beginning. Second, building as giving. Over generations, kings, queens, officials and ordinary families built on the plain. In Buddhist teaching, generous giving makes merit, good that ripens in this life and in lives to come, and a temple was a great gift to make. Inscriptions left by donors survive, and some record their wishes: to meet a future Buddha, to reach nibbana, to share the merit with their parents and with all beings. Third, the inside. Some temples are not solid mounds at all. You can walk into them, through dim corridors painted with scenes from the Buddha's past lives, past rows of seated Buddhas lit by small windows. Fourth, the plain today. Earthquakes have shaken Bagan, and some temples have cracked, fallen or been rebuilt. It is still a place of devotion: people make offerings, light candles and walk barefoot through the corridors. A plain of temples is what happens when people, over a long time, each decide to give something that will outlast them.
screen: `A KING, A MONK, A WAR.` · `EACH TEMPLE A GIFT.` · `PAINTED CORRIDORS INSIDE.` · `SHAKEN, REBUILT, STILL VISITED.` · then, large: `A PLAIN OF TEMPLES.`

On each out-breath, let a good wish go out from you, as the donors did, toward someone you love, or toward everyone.
Bagan. The plain beside the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, where kings and ordinary families built temples and stupas, gift after gift. Today's word.

886.title: Shwedagon
886.hook: the golden stupa of Yangon, said to hold hairs of the Buddha
886.howItsDone: Visitors to the Shwedagon climb barefoot, walk clockwise around the stupa, offer flowers, candles and gold leaf, and pour water over the Buddha image at the shrine for the day of the week they were born.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bagan, built gift by gift on a plain in Myanmar. Your line: a plain of temples.

Shoes off at the bottom of the stairs. Everyone climbs barefoot. At the top, a wide platform opens out around a great golden stupa, shaped like a bell, narrowing to a spire, blazing in the afternoon sun and ringed by smaller shrines. People walk around it slowly, clockwise. Some sit to meditate. Some chant. Some pour water over a small Buddha image at a corner shrine. This is the Shwedagon, in Yangon.
screen: `SHOES OFF, CLIMB BAREFOOT.` → `A GOLDEN BELL AGAINST THE SKY.` → `THE SHWEDAGON.`

segments.voice: First, the story. The Vinaya tells of two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, who meet the Buddha soon after his awakening, offer him food, and become his first lay followers. Later tradition adds what the Vinaya doesn't say: the Buddha gave them hairs from his head. Burmese tradition says they carried them home, where the hairs were enshrined on a hill. That hill is where the Shwedagon stands. Second, the gold. The stupa is covered in gold, given over generations by rulers and ordinary people; tradition at the site remembers a queen who gave her own weight in gold. Visitors still press small squares of gold leaf onto Buddha images. The shine is made of gifts. Third, the corners. Around the base are shrines for the days of the week, by the Burmese way of counting them. People go to the shrine for the day they were born, pour water over the Buddha image there, and make offerings, so each person on the platform brings something of their own: their birthday, their family's wishes, their troubles. Fourth, the stupa itself. Like the stupas of Sanchi, it is a reliquary, a mound built around something precious, and walking around it clockwise, keeping it on the right, is a way of honoring what is inside. Nobody sees the hairs. As at Kandy, people honor what they cannot see, and what they bring is gold, water, flowers, and the simple act of walking around.

887.title: Sukhothai
887.hook: the Thai kingdom whose walking Buddha images seem to move
887.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and lay meditators often practice walking meditation, pacing slowly along a short path, and walking Buddha images in the Sukhothai style are still made and honored in Thailand.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shwedagon, circled barefoot and clockwise. Your line: the golden stupa.

A bronze figure, caught mid-stride. The right heel is just lifting off the ground. One hand is raised, palm out. The body leans a little, the way a body leans when it is really walking and not posing for anyone. The robe clings to the legs as if a breeze had caught it. This week has already brought Buddhas carved in rock, sitting, standing and lying down. This one is going somewhere. Sculptors in an old Thai kingdom made images like this, and people who stand in front of them say the bronze seems to move.
screen: `A BRONZE BUDDHA, MID-STRIDE.` → `THE HEEL IS LIFTING.` → `THE BRONZE SEEMS TO MOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Sukhothai is the name of a kingdom and its old capital, in what is now Thailand. Its ruins still stand among trees and ponds: brick temple platforms, stupas, and rows of seated Buddhas, with the walking ones among them. Its kings supported Theravada monks, the same stream of teaching that reached Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Second, the story people see in the stride. Tradition tells that the Buddha once spent a rainy season in Tavatimsa heaven, teaching his mother, who had died soon after his birth. When the season ended, he came back down to earth by a stairway, with crowds waiting at the bottom. Some readers see that very moment in the walking image: the Buddha stepping down to meet people again. Third, walking was practice, not just travel. In the old suttas, monks pace back and forth on a short path, and the Buddha walks it too. The Pali word is cankama, walking up and down. One discourse praises it in plain terms: it helps you bear long journeys, it helps your food digest, and the calm you find while walking tends to last. Fourth, the face. On a walking Buddha it is not hurrying. The body moves; the face stays quiet: a mind that can stay still while the feet keep going. A day is full of moving, from the bed to the kettle, from the door to the bus. Sukhothai's bronze makes a claim about all of it: calm doesn't wait for you to sit down.
screen: `SUKHOTHAI: AN OLD THAI KINGDOM.` · `STEPPING DOWN FROM TAVATIMSA HEAVEN.` · `CANKAMA: WALKING AS PRACTICE.` · `A QUIET FACE ON A MOVING BODY.` · then, large: `THE WALKING BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: Find a few steps of clear floor, or if you can't walk right now, rest your hands on your knees and do it in your mind. Lift one heel slowly, feel the weight roll forward, let the foot touch down, then the other, and at the end of your short path pause, turn and come back, arms loose and face soft like the bronze.
Sukhothai. The old Thai kingdom whose sculptors cast the Buddha walking, heel lifting, face at rest. Today's word.
Your line: the walking Buddha. The feet keep going; the face stays quiet. That's day eight hundred eighty-seven.

888.title: Angkor
888.hook: Jayavarman VII, a Buddhist king of Cambodia, and the smiling faces of the Bayon
888.howItsDone: Cambodian Buddhists and visitors from many places come to the Bayon at Angkor Thom, and in Mahayana Buddhism Avalokiteshvara is honored as the bodhisattva of compassion, often called on in chant and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sukhothai, and the Buddha cast mid-stride. Your line: the walking Buddha.

Climb the steep stone steps of the Bayon, at the heart of the old city of Angkor Thom in Cambodia, and the faces find you before you find them. A great stone face on a tower, eyes half closed, lips turned up at the corners. Turn your head, and there's another, looking off in a different direction. Then another, on the next tower over. Moss in the cracks, lichen on the cheeks, and still that same calm, closed-mouth smile. Visitors have argued for a long time about whose face it is.
screen: `THE STEPS OF THE BAYON.` → `A FACE ON EVERY TOWER.` → `WHOSE FACE IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, the king. Angkor was the seat of a great Khmer kingdom, and kings there had built huge temples, some of them for Hindu gods, like Vishnu at Angkor Wat. King Jayavarman the Seventh was a Buddhist, of the Mahayana stream, and when he built his walled city he put the Bayon at its center. Second, the question nobody can settle. The temple left no label on the faces. Some scholars see the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, called Lokeshvara in Cambodia. Some see the king himself. Some see both at once: a ruler who wanted to be seen as compassion turned in every direction. The honest answer: nobody knows, and the stone doesn't say. Third, the bodhisattva behind the guess. In the Lotus Sutra, Avalokiteshvara is the one who hears beings who call out in trouble and comes to help, taking whatever form will reach them. A face turned to every point of the compass fits that picture well. Fourth, what the king's own words add. Inscriptions from his reign tell of hospitals and rest houses he founded, and one hospital inscription says, in substance, that the suffering of his people was his own pain. A king can say beautiful things, and historians weigh them carefully. But it is the same idea as the towers: a face that doesn't look away. And the smile itself? It isn't laughing at anything, or grinning for a camera. It has nowhere in particular to point: gentle, a little inward, offered to whoever happens to be standing there.
screen: `JAYAVARMAN VII, A BUDDHIST KING AT ANGKOR.` · `WHOSE FACES? NOBODY CAN SAY FOR SURE.` · `LOKESHVARA HEARS THOSE WHO CALL.` · `THEIR SUFFERING WAS HIS PAIN.` · then, large: `THE SMILING TOWERS.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes half close like the faces on the towers, and let the corners of your mouth lift just slightly, not a grin, not for anyone. Breathe in and out with the small smile, noticing the eyes, the jaw, the shoulders, and if it fades or feels strange, let it return without fuss.
Angkor. The old Khmer capital in Cambodia, where King Jayavarman the Seventh raised the Bayon and its towers of quiet, smiling faces. Today's word.
Your line: the smiling towers. Whose face it is, the stone still keeps to itself. Day eight hundred eighty-eight, done.

889.title: Luang Prabang's dawn
889.hook: the daily alms round in Laos, monks in a long saffron line
889.howItsDone: In Laos and other Theravada countries, monks walk an alms round early in the morning, and lay people kneel or stand by the road to place rice and other food in their bowls, often in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angkor's smiling towers. This week: stone Buddhas, a tooth kept safe, a plain of temples, a golden stupa and a walking Buddha. Your line: the smiling towers.

It's still dark in the old town of Luang Prabang, in Laos. Along the curb, people kneel on small mats, shoes off, a covered basket of warm sticky rice beside each of them. Then, from down the road, a line of monks appears, walking barefoot, single file, in saffron robes, each with a bowl held in front. Nobody calls out. Nobody bargains. A monk pauses for a breath at each person, the lid of the bowl lifts, a small ball of rice goes in, and the line moves on. By the time the sky turns pale, it's over.
screen: `BEFORE LIGHT, PEOPLE KNEEL BY THE ROAD.` → `A SAFFRON LINE, BOWLS IN HAND.` → `RICE IN, AND ON TO THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: First, the name for it. In Pali it's pindapata, the alms round: walking for food that is given. Monks in the Theravada tradition receive their meals from lay people rather than buying them, so this walk is not a show put on for the morning. It is how the monastery eats. Second, the bowl takes what is given. A monk on alms round doesn't ask, point, or choose. He stands, receives, and walks on. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, has a picture for this: "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village." Take a little, harm nothing, move along. Third, giving goes both ways. The person on the mat is practicing too. Giving is called dana, and the Buddha taught it to lay people as a practice in its own right. A short discourse in the Itivuttaka says householders support monks with robes, food and shelter, and monks support householders with the teaching, so each holds the other up. Fourth, guests at the edge. The alms round now draws visitors with cameras too. Local monks and community leaders have asked visitors to keep a respectful distance, stay quiet, and not give unless they mean it and know how. Some things are only beautiful when nobody turns them into a spectacle.
screen: `PINDAPATA: THE ALMS ROUND.` · `THE BOWL TAKES WHAT IS GIVEN.` · `GIVING HOLDS BOTH SIDES UP.` · `GUESTS KEEP A QUIET DISTANCE.` · then, large: `THE LINE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Picture a cool street just before dawn, a mat under your knees and warm rice in a basket, and hear bare feet coming down the road, almost silent. Watch one bowl stop in front of you, notice what it's like simply to give, without a word, without thanks, without a photo, then let the line move on into the pale light.
Pindapata. The alms round in the old town of Laos: monks walking in a saffron line, people kneeling to give rice. Today's word.
Your line: the line at dawn. Rice goes into the bowl, and the teaching comes back. See you tomorrow.
